title: ‘Doing it tough’: Diesel shock puts brakes on Super Retail sales
full_text:
Super Retail Group’s new chief quickly saw shoppers hit the brakes when diesel flirted with $3 a litre, prompting many of its core customers – fishermen, campers and four-wheel drivers – to stay at home.
Now with petrol prices once again rising, pushed by the protracted war in the Middle East and the removal of fuel excise relief by the Albanese government, the cost-of-living spectre has returned to haunt Super Retail’s chains including Supercheap Auto, Rebel, BCF and Macpac brands.
“We saw it when fuel prices went over $3, diesel specifically, we saw the demand come off and you can see it now with diesel prices just tipping over $2.50 … and that has had an impact on consumer confidence, there is no doubt about it,” Super Retail Group chief executive Paul Bradshaw told The Australian on Thursday.
This hurt sales and profitability for the retailer, which is particularly exposed to outdoor activities and car usage.
On Thursday Super Retail, which is trying to rebuild its reputation after dumping chief executive Anthony Heraghty last year, reported a 7.2 per cent drop in annual net profit to $205.9m as consumers pulled back on spending.
Group sales rose 3.2 per cent to $4.2bn for the year ended June 27 from a year earlier, with like-for-like sales up 1.8 per cent.
Super Retail trimmed its final dividend to 33c a share, fully franked and payable on September 29, down from 34c.
Sporting chain Rebel received a boost as football fans snapped up jerseys and footballs during the FIFA World Cup, as well as growing interest in getting fit and healthy.
Super Retail’s volumes for FIFA World Cup merchandise were up 70 per cent against the previous tournament four years ago, and sold out, with the licenced merchandise typically delivering stronger margins. Its annual like-for-like sales were up 3.8 per cent.
But it also faced challenges from poor weather that hit camping goods sales at its boating, camping and fishing chain BCF, as well as an algae outbreak in South Australia and Victoria that hurt demand for fishing products.
However, an earnings beat and what analysts saw as a “reasonable” start to trading for fiscal 2027 given the malaise swamping retailers saw Super Retail shares rocket 15 per cent to close at a five-month high of $14.45.
The $2.84bn company joins a raft of retailers to warn that fragile consumers were reining in their spending.
“I think the consumer is doing it really tough and I don’t see that changing in the near term,” Mr Bradshaw said.
Over the 2026 financial year its Supercheap Auto chain booked a 2.7 per cent rise in annual like-for-like sales, as customers looked to repair their cars and add new accessories. There was also good demand for tools and equipment.
Outdoor clothing and equipment chain Macpac’s like-for-like sales rose 1.5 per cent, but BCF’s fell 2.1 per cent.
For the first seven weeks of 2027, group like-for-like sales were up 1.5 per cent, driven by Supercheap Auto. Its like-for-like sales were up 4 per cent.
Rebel’s like-for-like sales rose 1.1 per cent, while BCF’s were up just 0.4 per cent. Macpac was the biggest loser, down 8.9 per cent, hurt by weak demand amid ongoing mild winter conditions over the peak trading period.
Barrenjoey’s head of consumer research Tom Kierath said beyond the numbers, the competitive landscape has intensified. “We think if the company can consistently deliver on its aim of mid-to-high single-digit profit growth, investors will reward it, though we aren’t sure that they have earned the right to embark on what looks like an aggressive store rollout, but time will tell,” Mr Kierath said.
